names.name: Ping'an fu
names.th: ผิงอันฝู (ยันต์ขอความสงบสุข)

etymology.root: Chinese 平安 píng'ān 'peace, safety' + 符 fú 'talisman, tally'
etymology.note: The second character is the same fu as in fulu, Taoist talismanic script: a fu was a tally, a thing split so the two halves match.

text.what: A sheet of yellow paper inscribed with sacred symbols, folded into a bagua shape or a rectangle and slipped into a red cloth sleeve. In Taiwan it is the commonest amulet there is: the little red pouch tucked in a wallet, the folded yellow-paper bagua hanging from a scooter key.
text.story:
The charm is obtained rather than bought outright, and the asking is specific. A worshipper offers incense, states their name, birthday and address and what they are asking for, and seeks the deity's permission with divination blocks. If it is granted, the talisman is raised above the main incense burner and circled clockwise three times — in the Taiwanese Gods account, to let it drink in the incense energy and switch on its power.

*Inference —* that sequence is worth reading closely. A name, a birth date and an address are the same details a registry takes; the charm is issued to a person, not to a pocket, and the censer is where it is stamped.

The writing on it belongs to the Taoist talismanic tradition, where the script is deliberately hard to read. Scholars including James Robson and Gil Raz have argued that the incomprehensibility of the written forms is central to a talisman's perceived authority, and Ge Hong wrote in the Baopuzi, in the Eastern Jin period, that successful use did not depend on the user being able to decipher the script.
text.how: Requested at a temple, activated over the censer, carried on the person, then retired on a calendar. A peace talisman is usually replaced once a year: before Lunar New Year the old one goes to the temple's furnace to be burned, and a fresh one is requested for the coming year.
text.today: Handed out at temples across Taiwan and kept in nearly every household there, as of the account read in September 2026 — in wallets, on scooter keys, in car glove boxes and in bags. Whether the charm on a scooter key is a devotional object or a habit is not a question this atlas settles; the temple's own procedure treats it as the former, and the wallet treats it as the latter.

dating.period: Taoist talismanic practice; the paper peace charm itself is undated in the sources read
dating.label: undated here; carried now
dating.note: The wider fu tradition is dated on this atlas's fu-talisman record, back to the Eastern Han and to Ge Hong's Baopuzi. Neither source read dates this particular charm, so no years are given here.

object.made_by: written at a temple, by or under a priest; issued to a named person after the deity's permission is asked
object.inscription: sacred symbols in Taoist talismanic script, which is not meant to be read by the carrier
object.note: No measurement is published in the sources read.

against.who: the Taiwanese Gods account, which describes the charm as carried on the person for safe passage
its own name — ping'an, peace and safety — and the yearly renewal that goes with it
Taoist talismanic practice generally, where most coin talismans ask Lei Gong to protect their carriers from evil spirits and misfortune
against.note: that sentence in the source is about coin talismans; it is given here as the tradition's framing, not as a claim read about this charm

kin.as: the class it belongs to — this is the ordinary, household end of Taoist talismanic writing
the tradition that writes it and the priesthood that keeps the script
the step that issues it: incense, a name, a birth date, divination blocks, three clockwise circles over the censer
its clock — one year, then the furnace
how it ends, at the temple, before Lunar New Year
Japan's sealed brocade pouch, taken from a shrine and returned to be burned a year later: the same cycle, the same year
the Japanese paper talisman descended from the same Taoist writing
the Korean paper charm from the same root, and the third of the three
the fixed version at the same door: this one rides in a pocket, that one is screwed above the lintel
the material that lets a temple issue thousands and burn them all a year later
